explanations.explanation: Right there in the opening line, Paul says he is “…an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God…” (Ephesians 1:1). He doesn't say he earned the title or campaigned for it. I've seen plenty of people puff up a job title, and Paul hands the credit upward instead. That's a good way to start a letter.

explanations.answer: By a vote of the church
explanations.explanation: Paul never mentions a vote here. No ballots, no clipboards, no committee meeting afterward with cookies. He says he is an apostle of Christ Jesus “…by the will of God…” (Ephesians 1:1). So the answer sits with God's will.

I respect hard work. I stamped cookies until my edges wore smooth. But that's not what Paul writes. He says he is an apostle of Christ Jesus “…by the will of God…” (Ephesians 1:1). He doesn't point to his own effort at all.

Paul says God “…has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms.” (Ephesians 1:3). Notice the little words "in Christ." Paul comes back to them again and again in this passage. Every spiritual blessing, and they're all found in Him.
Moses doesn't show up anywhere in this verse. Paul says the blessing comes “…in Christ…” (Ephesians 1:3). Every spiritual blessing is found in Him.
David isn't in this verse either. Paul says God has blessed us “…in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms.” (Ephesians 1:3). Paul puts the blessing in Christ.

explanations.answer: Holy and blameless in His presence
explanations.explanation: Paul says God chose us “…to be holy and blameless in His presence.” (Ephesians 1:4). Look at where that happens: in His presence. And the choosing happened before the foundation of the world.

explanations.answer: Rulers over every nation on earth
explanations.explanation: That one sounds impressive, I'll give you that. But Paul never says it in this verse. He says God chose us “…to be holy and blameless in His presence.” (Ephesians 1:4). The crowns can stay in the box.

explanations.answer: Teachers of the law in every city
explanations.explanation: Teaching the law in every city? That's a lot of miles, baker, and Paul never hands out that job in this verse. He says God chose us “…to be holy and blameless in His presence.” (Ephesians 1:4). This verse is about being in His presence, not about a job.

Paul says God “…predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ…” (Ephesians 1:5). Adoption means being brought into a family. I think that's why this word hits so warm. It comes through Jesus Christ, and Paul ties it to the good pleasure of God's will.

Hired servants clock in and clock out, and that's not the word Paul picks. He says God predestined us “…for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ…” (Ephesians 1:5). That's family, not a payroll. I'd take the family.

Soldiers? Somebody's marching a little early, baker. Paul doesn't use that picture in this verse. He says God predestined us “…for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ…” (Ephesians 1:5). The word he chose is adoption, and that's a family word.

Verse 4 ends with the words “In love,” and verse 5 runs right on: “He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ…” (Ephesians 1:4-5). So the predestining happens in love. Paul doesn't give it any other setting. I think that's a lovely thing to see tucked at the end of a verse.

This one is true, and the text says so. Verse 4 ends with “In love,” and verse 5 goes straight on: “He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ…” (Ephesians 1:4-5). It's easy to miss because the verse break lands right in the middle. I've missed things between two pages more than once.

Paul says it is “…to the praise of His glorious grace, which He has freely given us in the Beloved One.” (Ephesians 1:6). Freely given is how Paul puts it. Then he goes on, “In Him we have redemption through His blood…” (Ephesians 1:7). The Beloved One is where it all comes from.
The law is a fine thing to praise, but Paul doesn't say it here. He says it's “…to the praise of His glorious grace…” (Ephesians 1:6). That grace is what God has freely given us in the Beloved One.

Strength is a good word, but it's not the one in this verse. Paul says it's “…to the praise of His glorious grace, which He has freely given us in the Beloved One.” (Ephesians 1:6). Grace is the word to hold onto.

Paul says, “In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses…” (Ephesians 1:7). Forgiveness. I know what it is to feel stuck in the dark, and this word is the light coming in. And Paul says it's according to the riches of His grace.

A record is something you keep and check, but that's not what Paul writes. He says, “In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses…” (Ephesians 1:7). Forgiveness is the word. That's much nicer than a filing cabinet.

Weight is a heavy word, but it's not the one Paul uses. He says, “In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses…” (Ephesians 1:7). The word is forgiveness, which is the opposite of carrying it around.

Paul says the opposite. He writes of “…the riches of His grace that He lavished on us with all wisdom and understanding.” (Ephesians 1:7-8). Lavished isn't a small, careful word. There's no sparing in it. I think a stingy hand would never earn that word.

Right, the text says the opposite of sparingly. Paul writes of “…the riches of His grace that He lavished on us with all wisdom and understanding.” (Ephesians 1:7-8). Lavished means poured out, not rationed. That's a generous God.

Paul says, “And He has made known to us the mystery of His will according to His good pleasure…” (Ephesians 1:9). A mystery that God hands over to us. That's a mystery with the lights turned on. It isn't kept in a locked drawer.

Hidden stuff, I know about. I spent years in the back of a drawer. But Paul says the opposite: “And He has made known to us the mystery of His will according to His good pleasure…” (Ephesians 1:9). God has made it known.

Paul doesn't say anything about angels in this verse. He says God “…has made known to us the mystery of His will according to His good pleasure…” (Ephesians 1:9). The word is us, and Paul is writing to the saints in Ephesus. So the sharing is with them.

explanations.answer: Bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ
explanations.explanation: Paul says it is “…a plan for the fullness of time, to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.” (Ephesians 1:10). All things, both heaven and earth, brought together. It's a very big plan. And it all centers on Christ.

explanations.answer: Keep the things of heaven apart from the things of earth
explanations.explanation: That's a plan for keeping everything separate, and Paul says the opposite. The plan is “…to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.” (Ephesians 1:10). Together, not apart. All things in heaven and on earth are brought together in Christ.

explanations.answer: Set every nation on earth under the law of Moses
explanations.explanation: Moses isn't mentioned in this verse, and neither is any law. Paul says the plan is “…to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.” (Ephesians 1:10). It's about being brought together in Christ.

explanations.answer: For the praise of His glory
explanations.explanation: Paul says it is “…in order that we, who were the first to hope in Christ, would be for the praise of His glory.” (Ephesians 1:12). The point lands on God's glory. Not on the ones who were chosen. I find that humbling, and I think it takes the pressure off.

explanations.answer: For the honor of their own names
explanations.explanation: I like seeing my name on a handle as much as anybody. But Paul doesn't say that. He says those who were first to hope in Christ would be “…for the praise of His glory.” (Ephesians 1:12). The praise goes to God's glory.

explanations.answer: For the judging of the nations
explanations.explanation: Judging the nations sounds like a heavy job, and it's not in this verse. Paul says those who were first to hope in Christ would be “…for the praise of His glory.” (Ephesians 1:12). The reason he gives is praise. I'll stick with my apron.

The order in the verse is the other way around. Paul says, “And in Him, having heard and believed the word of truth…” and only then, “…you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit…” (Ephesians 1:13). First hearing and believing, then the sealing. Hearing came first.

Right, the sealing comes after. Paul says, “And in Him, having heard and believed the word of truth…” and then, “…you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit…” (Ephesians 1:13). So they heard the gospel first, and believed it. The sealing follows.

Paul says the Holy Spirit “…is the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God’s possession, to the praise of His glory.” (Ephesians 1:14). A pledge is like a promise you can hold now. And the inheritance is still being waited on. I like that the Spirit is the pledge.

Wages are what you collect after a hard shift, and that's not Paul's word here. He says the Holy Spirit is “…the pledge of our inheritance…” (Ephesians 1:14). An inheritance is given, not clocked in for.

A harvest is a nice picture, but Paul doesn't use it here. He says the Holy Spirit “…is the pledge of our inheritance…” (Ephesians 1:14). The word is inheritance, and Paul says the Spirit is the pledge until the redemption of those who are God's possession.

Paul says the Spirit is the pledge of our inheritance “…until the redemption of those who are God’s possession, to the praise of His glory.” (Ephesians 1:14). So they're God's own possession. That's a happy thing to be called. It's a bit like being a cookie that belongs in the box.

The text says it plainly. Paul writes of “…the redemption of those who are God’s possession, to the praise of His glory.” (Ephesians 1:14). So the ones redeemed are His possession. It's easy to stumble on that word, since it's tucked near the end.
